chapter_title: Concerning the worn and torn apart Garments, or th

fills.fill: at the foundation of the earths
fills.notes: The rags (devoured light) are said to be entangled in the three earths below, but still positioned relative to the Porter, who stands at the base/border of the cosmos. The substrate regularly locates mixed light ‘below’ yet ‘above the head’ of the boundary-keeper; the missing phrase most naturally gives the cosmic place: the base/foundation region where the earths are set.

fills.fill: for it is torn from its first garments and cast down
fills.notes: The naming ‘rags’ is explained by correspondential function: light that should clothe/shine is now rent, separated from its proper integuments, and reduced to tatters through mixture and violence. This matches the next broken clause about something being ‘set’.

fills.fill: and set in the altered forms of the rulers
fills.notes: The reason they are ‘rags’ is not moral but ontological: the enlightening power is fixed (‘set’) into alien shapes—i.e., the rulers’ forms in firmaments/earths. This anticipates ¶15’s explicit language of ‘altered forms’ and ‘many names’.
The clause resumes a catalogue of names already ‘proclaimed’ (cf. ¶9 “which we have proclaimed”). The parallel phrasing is characteristic of this substrate’s classificatory style.

The sense demands the full term: the ‘elements’ are defined as the power remaining below, rising in wombs of the earths and flowing into all things—i.e., elemental mixture as the ultimate vessel of bound life/light.

In the oldest cosmological register the Light-Cross is not primarily a salvific symbol but the ‘extension’/‘stretching’ of bound light through the cosmos, like a spanning framework holding the mixed powers in their places.

The final location phrase ‘in the dry and the moist’ points to vegetation and generative nature (dry land / moist waters). The Light-Cross as bound light ‘upon the earth’ is correspondentially in all germination and growth.

fills.fill: in the wombs of the fruits
fills.notes: The slain soul is specified as the life-power in fruit/vegetables/seeds. The natural ‘womb’ where this power is killed and harvested is their inner generative place; this also links back to ¶11’s ‘wombs of all the earths’.
The sentence sums up the preceding nomenclature; the substrate often closes a list with ‘these names that we have proclaimed’.
What all names denote is one underlying reality: a single ‘power’ (living/enlightening power) that is later said to enlighten and to have been divided in the first contest.

The logic requires: one power ‘since the beginning’; then ‘it … as it enlightens’, before separation into parts in the first contest. ‘was one’ completes the ontological unity claim in the oldest layer.

assessment: Most gaps can be constrained by the chapter’s internal correspondential structure: (1) the repeated taxonomic formula (‘we have termed/proclaimed’), (2) the cosmological placement around the Porter and the three earths, and (3) the governing thesis in ¶15 that all these named states are one enlightening power divided by the first contest. Two restorations in ¶8 and ¶14 remain tentative because the surviving context signals explanation-by-correspondence but does not uniquely fix the exact wording.
